metadata.title: Finding the contextual impacts on Students’ Mathematical performance using a Machine Learning-based Approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 mathematics data for Morocco, combining student, teacher, and school files via IEA IDB Analyzer (v5.0). The authors report removing ID-related variables and weight/file-maintenance variables from the explanatory feature pool, but they do not state that complex survey weights were applied in model estimation. Because the analysis is based on standard supervised ML classifiers (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost) and the manuscript does not describe any weight-aware training or replicate-weight variance estimation, the most defensible interpretation is that models were trained without TIMSS sampling weights. The analytic sample was further restricted by deleting variables with >10% missingness and imputing remaining missing values using scikit-learn’s SimpleImputer (mode), after which the final feature set contained 400 variables.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variable is a majority-vote categorical benchmark derived from TIMSS PV-based achievement levels (Low vs Others), rather than a PV-based continuous achievement score. Missing-data handling is reported via SimpleImputer, which replaces missing values with mode values for categorical variables; this is treated as mean_imputation in the schema mapping because the paper does not provide a separate literal for mode-based imputation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The authors used TIMSS 2019 Morocco Grade 8 mathematics data and combined student, teacher, and school records using IEA IDB Analyzer (v5.0), starting from 8458 entries. They created the response variable by taking TIMSS PV-based achievement benchmark categories and applying a majority vote to assign each student to a single class; ties were removed (68 tied cases), yielding 8390 students. For preprocessing, they removed 300 variables (IDs/weights/file maintenance and redundant variables; variables with 100% missingness; and numerical scale-score indices that were considered redundant with categorical indices). They also removed PV/benchmark variables from predictors (keeping only the newly generated response benchmark BSMIBM) and deleted 74 variables with missingness rates >10%. Missing values in the remaining dataset were imputed using SimpleImputer, and the final dataset contained 400 variables.

main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics achievement (Low vs Others; majority-vote benchmark BSMIBM)
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost — Accuracy: 81.92, F1-score: 74.42. SVM — Accuracy: 65.87, F1-score: 16.03. Random Forest — Accuracy: 79.18, F1-score: 65.39.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Morocco) the study leveraged mathematics achievement too low, classroom libraries, science achievement too low, work on your own, and student confident in mathematics to classify students into Low vs Others, finding that XGBoost achieved the highest accuracy (81.92) and F1-score (74.42) compared with SVM and Random Forest. This indicates that strengthening student confidence and independent practice, alongside improving instructional resources and classroom learning environments, may improve the identification and support of low-achieving Moroccan students, though the results are predictive and not causal and were obtained without documented PV-based continuous-score modeling.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 mathematics data for Morocco (final analytic sample: 8,390 students) to classify students’ mathematics achievement into Low vs Others using a majority-vote benchmark derived from TIMSS PV-based achievement levels (response variable BSMIBM). After preprocessing (removing ID/weight variables, deleting variables with 100% missingness, removing predictors with >10% missingness, and imputing remaining missing values with SimpleImputer), the authors trained three supervised ML classifiers: SVM, Random Forest, and XGBoost. XGBoost performed best, reaching 81.92% accuracy and an F1-score of 74.42, outperforming Random Forest (79.18%, 65.39) and SVM (65.87%, 16.03). The top contextual factors highlighted by XGBoost feature importance include student confidence, independent work frequency, time spent on math instruction, and effects of resource shortages. Limitations include the use of a dichotomized benchmark rather than continuous PV scores, lack of reported survey-weighted estimation, and the fact that feature importance supports prediction rather than causal claims.
